title: Block 3 Practice Test 1
context: Foundations of Medicine, Block 3, Weeks 9 to 12

questions.p: Elsie, 71, has fatigue that is worse in winter. Her blood film shows red cells clustered together in large groups, not in stacked chains. Which mechanism explains this film?
o: Paraproteins neutralize red cell surface charge
Microthrombi break the red cells into pieces
Lost membrane remodels the cells into spheres
IgM tetramers link many red cells together
questions.e:
Correct: D. Large clusters are agglutination, seen in cold AIHA, the IgM-mediated hemolysis in your Week 9 Jeopardy deck. IgM tetramers link many red cells together.
A: Charge neutralization by excess protein causes rouleaux, the stacked chains.
B: Microthrombi form schistocytes.
C: Membrane loss and remodelling form spherocytes.
Takeaway: Agglutination means IgM. Rouleaux means excess protein.

questions.p: Ruth, 66, has newly diagnosed AML with a very high blast count. She is short of breath, confused and has a headache. Which diagnosis and treatment fit?
o: Leukostasis, treated with IV fluids and leukapheresis
Tumour lysis syndrome, treated with rasburicase
Febrile neutropenia, treated with IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
questions.e:
Correct: A. Big, sticky blasts get stuck in small vessels and cause hypoxia, confusion and headache. Leukostasis is managed with IV fluids, leukapheresis and cytoreduction.
B: TLS causes electrolyte derangements and renal failure.
C: Hypercalcemia is a myeloma complication.
D: Febrile neutropenia needs a fever with low neutrophils.
Takeaway: Leukostasis is a medical emergency in AML and ALL.

questions.p: Walter, 81, has eaten very little for several weeks after a stroke. He now bruises easily. INR is 2.6, aPTT is normal, platelets and fibrinogen are normal and he takes no anticoagulant. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e:
Correct: B. An isolated high INR points to the extrinsic pathway and factor VII. Vitamin K deficiency is a listed acquired cause, and poor intake fits.
A: VWD can prolong the aPTT, and the INR is normal.
C: FXIII deficiency bleeds with a normal INR and aPTT.
D: Hemophilia A prolongs the aPTT with a normal INR.
Takeaway: Isolated high INR: factor VII, warfarin, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease.

questions.p: Noah, 6, has newly diagnosed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. His parents ask what treatment will involve. Which description is correct?
o: 7+3 induction, with treatment over in 4-6 months
A tyrosine kinase inhibitor taken daily for life
2-3 years of chemotherapy with CNS prophylaxis
Surgery and radiation as the main curative tools
questions.e:
Correct: C. ALL treatment runs 2 to 3 years on the Dana-Farber protocol: induction, consolidation and low-dose maintenance, plus CNS prophylaxis by LP or radiation. About 90% of children are cured.
A: 7+3 induction over 4 to 6 months is the AML timeline.
B: A daily TKI is chronic treatment for CML.
D: Radiation and surgery are not treatment options for acute leukemia.
Takeaway: Children with ALL: 90% cured.

questions.p: A man with a ruptured spleen is in a massive transfusion and needs replacement of all his clotting factors. The product is stored in a freezer and must be thawed before use. Which product is it?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Plasma contains all coagulation factors. It is stored at -18°C for up to 1 year and takes about 20 minutes to thaw.
A: Fibrinogen concentrate replaces fibrinogen only.
B: Platelets are stored at room temperature for up to 7 days, as in your Week 10 quiz.
C: PCC holds the vitamin K dependent factors.
D: Cryoprecipitate is also frozen, but it holds FVIII, FXIII, vWF and fibrinogen, not all factors.
Takeaway: Room temperature: platelets and fibrinogen concentrate. Fridge: red cells. Freezer: plasma and cryo.

questions.p: Frank, 60, smokes heavily and has obstructive sleep apnea. Hb is 182 g/L with normal WBC and platelets. JAK2 is negative and EPO is high. What is the best approach?
o: Treat the cause of his hypoxia
Phlebotomy alone to lower his hematocrit
questions.e:
Correct: A. A high EPO with a negative JAK2 is secondary erythrocytosis. Systemic hypoxia from smoking or OSA is a listed cause, and treatment targets the cause.
B: Imatinib treats CML.
C: Phlebotomy to a hematocrit below 0.45 is PV management.
D: Hydroxyurea is cytoreduction for high-risk PV.
Takeaway: Secondary erythrocytosis: find and treat the cause.

questions.p: Priya, 34, has heavy periods. Hb is 104 g/L, MCV 76 fL and ferritin is low. She feels well, has no bowel symptoms and eats a mixed diet. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Red cell transfusion to correct her Hb today
IV iron sucrose to refill her stores quickly
Erythropoietin injections until Hb is normal
Oral iron and work-up of her heavy periods
questions.e:
Correct: D. Iron deficiency management is to replace iron and find the cause. IV iron is kept for inadequate absorption or rapid blood loss, and she has neither.
A: Transfusion is for Hb below 70 g/L or symptomatic anemia, and she is well at 104 g/L.
B: IV iron is for poor absorption or rapid loss, as for Robert after gastric bypass in your Week 9 quiz.
C: EPO is for renal failure, AIDS on antivirals, chemotherapy, pre-op care and MDS.
Takeaway: Replace the iron and find the source of the loss.

questions.p:
Albert, 79, has lower-risk MDS on IPSS. Which belong in his management?
i) Red cell transfusion when Hb falls below 70 g/L
ii) Growth factor support with EPO or G-CSF
iii) Monitoring and treating iron overload
iv) Hypomethylating agents to slow progression
questions.e:
Correct: C. Lower-risk MDS care aims at quality of life: transfusions below 70 g/L, managing iron overload and growth factor support.
A: Hypomethylating agents such as azacitidine belong to higher-risk care.
B: This leaves out iron overload, which transfused patients need watched.
D: Statement iv) is higher-risk management.
Takeaway: Lower risk: support. Higher risk: change the course.

questions.p: Dennis, 52, has itchy skin after hot baths and a ruddy face. Hb is 185 g/L and JAK2 V617F is positive. Which result fits the minor criterion for his most likely diagnosis?
o: A platelet count of 450 or more
questions.e:
Correct: B. Aquagenic pruritus, a ruddy complexion, a high Hb and JAK2 fit polycythemia vera. Its minor criterion is a subnormal serum EPO.
A: Palpable splenomegaly is a minor criterion for primary myelofibrosis.
C: A platelet count of 450 or more is the first major criterion for ET.
D: A high EPO points to secondary erythrocytosis.
Takeaway: Low EPO is primary. Normal or high EPO is secondary.

questions.p: Leonard, 70, is on hemodialysis for kidney failure. He has a new proximal DVT. Which anticoagulant is the best long-term choice for him?
questions.e:
Correct: B. Warfarin is the listed DVT treatment for patients with renal failure. LMWH, fondaparinux and the direct Xa inhibitors are cleared by the kidney, and their half-life lengthens in renal failure.
A: Rivaroxaban is renally cleared.
C: Dalteparin is renally cleared, and its half-life lengthens in renal failure.
D: Fondaparinux is renally cleared.
Takeaway: LMWH for cancer and pregnancy. Warfarin for renal failure.

questions.p: Gloria, 70, has pneumonia. WBC is 24 with mostly neutrophils that show toxic granules and Döhle bodies. There are no blasts or promyelocytes, and eosinophils and basophils are normal. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.e:
Correct: C. Toxic granules and Döhle bodies without myeloblasts or promyelocytes point to a secondary, reactive neutrophilia. Infection causes a left shift.
A: CML shows basophilia, eosinophilia and immature myeloid cells, as in your Week 11 quiz.
B: AML shows blasts.
D: CLL is a lymphocytosis of mature B cells.
Takeaway: Blasts, basophils, eosinophils and clonality point to a primary cause.

questions.p: Mia, 26, had radiation to her neck and mediastinum for Hodgkin lymphoma 3 months ago. When she bends her neck forward, she feels electric tingling down her arms and legs. Which explanation fits?
o: Radiation pericarditis, inflaming the heart sac
Transient demyelination of the spinal cord
questions.e:
Correct: D. Paresthesia into the arms and legs on neck flexion is L'Hermitte's sign, a subacute effect from transient demyelination of the spinal cord.
A: Pneumonitis causes fever, cough and dyspnea 6 to 12 weeks after mediastinal RT.
B: Hypothyroidism is a late effect and does not cause tingling on neck flexion.
C: Pericarditis is inflammation of the sac around the heart.
Takeaway: Subacute: pneumonitis, pericarditis, L'Hermitte's sign. Late: hypothyroidism, infertility, second cancers.

questions.p: Samir, 40, has mild calf pain after being kicked in a soccer game. His Wells score is 0, so DVT is unlikely. What is the best first investigation?
questions.e:
Correct: A. With DVT unlikely (score of 1 or less), a negative D-dimer excludes the diagnosis.
B: Venogram is the invasive gold standard, not a first test.
C: CTPA investigates pulmonary embolism.
D: Ultrasound comes first when pretest probability is high, as in your Schulich review case.
Takeaway: Negative D-dimer rules out. A positive one means nothing on its own.

questions.p: In a trial, a new drug lowers the relapse rate from 20% in the control group to 15% in the treatment group. What are the absolute risk reduction and the number needed to treat?
questions.e:
Correct: C. ARR is control risk minus treatment risk: 20% minus 15% is 5%. NNT is the number treated to prevent one event: 1 divided by 0.05 is 20.
A: NNT is 1 divided by 0.05, which is 20.
B: 15% is the risk in the treatment group.
D: 25% is the relative risk reduction (5 divided by 20), not the ARR.
Takeaway: NNT = 1 / ARR.

questions.p: Gordon, 64, is on day 7 of unfractionated heparin after hip surgery. His platelets fall from 260 to 95 and he develops a new leg DVT. He is not bleeding. What is the best next step?
o: Switch to dalteparin and recheck platelets
Give platelets and continue the heparin
Start warfarin now and stop the heparin
Stop all heparin and start argatroban
questions.e:
Correct: D. A platelet fall 5 to 10 days into heparin with a new thrombosis fits HIT. Stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban or fondaparinux.
A: Dalteparin is a heparin, so it must stop too.
B: Platelet transfusions are avoided in HIT.
C: Warfarin starts only once platelets normalize.
Takeaway: HIT causes thrombosis, not bleeding.

questions.p: Amira, 52, has septic shock and is oozing from her line sites. Platelets are 35, INR 2.0, fibrinogen 0.7 g/L and D-dimer is high. Hb is 92 g/L. Which set of blood products fits her bleeding?
o: Platelets with packed red cells, no plasma
Red cells, plasma and vitamin K
Plasma with IV vitamin K only
questions.e:
Correct: B. This is DIC. For bleeding, give cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen is below 1.0, platelets if below 50 and plasma if INR is above 1.5. Her Hb is above the red cell threshold of 70 to 80.
A: She also needs fibrinogen and factors, and her Hb does not need red cells.
C: She does not need red cells at 92 g/L, and vitamin K is for warfarin or vitamin K deficiency.
D: Plasma alone leaves her fibrinogen and platelets low.
Takeaway: DIC: consumption of factors and platelets, so low fibrinogen, as in your Week 10 quiz.

questions.p:
Which are palliative uses of radiation therapy?
i) Spinal cord compression
ii) Superior vena cava syndrome
iii) Bleeding from a GI or gynecologic tumour
iv) CNS prophylaxis in ALL
questions.e:
Correct: B. Cord compression, vascular compression such as SVC syndrome and tumour bleeding are listed palliative uses.
A: CNS prophylaxis in ALL is a curative use.
C: This leaves out tumour bleeding.
D: Statement iv) is a curative use.
Takeaway: Radiation cures limited disease and palliates compression and bleeding.

questions.p: A 10-day-old boy has oozing from his umbilical stump and bleeds for days after circumcision. Platelet count, PT/INR, aPTT and fibrinogen are all normal. Which test is most likely to make the diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: C. Bleeding with a normal INR and aPTT has a short list that includes FXIII deficiency, as in your Week 10 quiz. A factor XIII assay is one of the follow-up tests.
A: D-dimers come from plasmin breaking down cross-linked fibrin and do not diagnose a factor deficiency.
B: Anti-Xa measures the activity of heparin and Xa inhibitors.
D: A mixing study works up a prolonged clotting time, and his are normal.
Takeaway: Normal INR and PTT with bleeding: platelets, VWD, FXIII, fibrinolysis, vessels.

questions.p: Sophie, 24, has classical Hodgkin lymphoma. Staging shows stage IIA disease with a bulky mediastinal mass. Which treatment plan fits best?
o: A full course, ABVD × 2 then AVD × 4
Watch and wait until B symptoms appear
A short course of chemotherapy, then radiation
questions.e:
Correct: A. Bulky disease is often treated like advanced stage. She gets the full course of ABVD × 2 then AVD × 4, with radiation if a PET-positive residual mass persists.
B: All Hodgkin patients are treated, aiming to cure.
C: A short course then involved-field radiation is for non-bulky stage I to II.
D: Chemotherapy is the main modality in Hodgkin lymphoma.
Takeaway: Bulky early stage Hodgkin is treated as advanced.

questions.p: Which pairing of antiplatelet drug and its target is correct?
questions.e:
Correct: D. Clopidogrel blocks the P2Y12 receptor pathway, which ADP from the dense granules acts on.
A: Clopidogrel acts on P2Y12, and aspirin is the drug that lowers thromboxane A2.
B: Abciximab is directed against glycoprotein IIb/IIIa.
C: Aspirin inhibits cyclooxygenase and lowers thromboxane A2.
Takeaway: Aspirin: COX. Clopidogrel: P2Y12. Abciximab: GPIIb/IIIa.

questions.p: A 70-year-old man arrives in hemorrhagic shock after a crash. His blood group is unknown and red cells are needed before testing can be done. Which group should the blood bank issue?
questions.e:
Correct: B. O negative is the universal red cell donor, but O positive is used for males and for women over 45. O negative is kept for women under 45.
A: AB negative is not a universal donor group.
C: O negative is kept for women under 45.
D: AB positive is the universal recipient, not the universal donor.
Takeaway: Red cells: O donor, AB recipient. Plasma: AB donor.

questions.p: Adam, 30, has an anterior mediastinal mass that has caused symptoms over several months. AFP is normal and beta-hCG is mildly raised. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.e:
Correct: A. An onset over months fits lymphoma or seminoma, and beta-hCG is raised in 10% of seminomas. AFP is the marker of non-seminomatous tumours.
B: Thymoma grows over years and is linked to anti-AChR.
C: Lymphoblastic lymphoma comes on over days.
D: Non-seminomatous tumours raise AFP in 60 to 80% and come on over days.
Takeaway: Days: lymphoblastic or NSGCT. Months: lymphoma, seminoma. Years: thymoma, teratoma.

questions.p: Hana, 16, has heavy periods and has had nosebleeds since childhood. Her mother bruises easily. Platelets and PT/INR are normal. A VWD screen shows a proportional drop in vWF antigen and activity. Which treatment fits her most likely subtype?
questions.e:
Correct: D. A proportional reduction in vWF antigen and activity is type 1 VWD, the most common form, treated with DDAVP. Tranexamic acid helps mucosal bleeding.
A: VWF/FVIII concentrate is for type 2 and type 3 VWD.
B: Vitamin K reverses warfarin and treats vitamin K deficiency.
C: Platelet transfusion is a treatment for platelet function disorders.
Takeaway: VWD is autosomal, so mothers and daughters can both bleed.

questions.p: Patient A, 47, has bleeding gums and petechiae. Her platelets are 12, and INR, PTT and fibrinogen are normal. Patient B, 47, has a swollen, painful knee from a bleed into the joint. His PTT is prolonged and his CBC is normal. Which type of hemostatic problem does each have, in order?
questions.e:
Correct: C. Mucosal bleeding with a low platelet count is a primary hemostatic problem. Deep bleeding with a prolonged PTT is a secondary problem.
A: Patient A has severe thrombocytopenia, which is primary.
B: This reverses the two patterns.
D: Patient B has a prolonged PTT and a normal platelet count, which is secondary.
Takeaway: Mucosal bleeding is more likely primary. Deep bleeding is more likely secondary.

questions.p: Which statement about fibrinolysis is correct?
o: Thrombin cross-links the fibrin monomers itself
TAFI speeds up the formation of plasmin
Plasmin breaks cross-linked fibrin to D-dimers
questions.e:
Correct: D. t-PA converts plasminogen to plasmin, which breaks down cross-linked fibrin into D-dimers.
A: Thrombin activates Factor XIII, and FXIII cross-links the fibrin monomers.
B: TAFI inhibits plasmin formation and suppresses fibrinolysis.
C: t-PA converts plasminogen. PAI-1 inhibits plasmin and t-PA.
Takeaway: Fibrinolysis: t-PA on. TAFI, anti-plasmin and PAI-1 off.

questions.p: Tyler, 28, has a single 0.8 cm soft, mobile, non-tender neck node found on exam. He has no fever, night sweats or weight loss, and his CBC is normal. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Fine needle aspirate with flow cytometry
Excisional biopsy of the node this week
PET-CT to stage a possible lymphoma
questions.e:
Correct: B. He has no concerning features, and a node must be over 1 cm to be tested clinically. In primary care, over 98% of enlarged nodes are non-malignant.
A: FNA is a biopsy, and the node is below the size for testing.
C: Biopsy is for nodes over 1 cm or with concerning features.
D: PET-CT stages a lymphoma once it is diagnosed.
Takeaway: Red flags: B symptoms, supraclavicular, generalized, fixed or matted.

questions.p: A 70-year-old man has a marrow core biopsy for anemia. Cellularity is reported as 30%. How is this best described?
o: Not assessable on a core biopsy
questions.e:
Correct: A. Marrow cellularity is about 100 minus age, so a 70-year-old should be about 30%.
B: Hypocellular is well below that, as in aplastic anemia.
C: Cellularity is assessed on the core biopsy.
D: Hypercellular is well above that, such as 80% in an 80-year-old in your Jeopardy deck.
Takeaway: Cellularity = 100 minus age.

questions.p: Vincristine is the O in CHOP-R. Which statement about how it works is correct?
o: It cross-links guanine and blocks S phase entry
It interferes with nucleic acid metabolism
It inhibits microtubule assembly in M phase
It inhibits topoisomerase II and intercalates DNA
questions.e:
Correct: C. Vincristine (Oncovin) is a vinca alkaloid. It inhibits microtubule assembly in metaphase and disrupts M phase.
A: Cross-linking guanine describes alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide.
B: Interfering with nucleic acid metabolism describes anti-metabolites such as methotrexate.
D: Topoisomerase II inhibition and intercalation describe anti-tumour antibiotics such as doxorubicin.
Takeaway: Know one mechanism per class.

questions.p: Doris, 78, takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. She arrives with a large GI bleed and an INR above 10. Consent is obtained. Which reversal plan is best?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Warfarin is reversed urgently with PCC. Vitamin K is given with it to prevent rebound coagulopathy when the PCC wears off.
A: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.
B: Andexanet alpha is for Xa inhibitors and is pending approval.
C: Protamine reverses heparin.
D: DDAVP treats mild hemophilia A and type 1 VWD, and cryoprecipitate replaces fibrinogen.
Takeaway: Warfarin reversal: PCC plus vitamin K.

questions.p:
A classmate thinks your patient's megaloblastic anemia is from folate deficiency. Which findings point to B12 deficiency instead?
i) A raised methylmalonic acid
ii) Loss of proprioception in the feet
iii) A raised homocysteine
iv) Hypersegmented neutrophils on the film
questions.e:
Correct: B. Methylmalonic acid rises only when B12 is low, and loss of proprioception is a B12 neurological feature.
A: Homocysteine rises in both deficiencies, so it does not separate them.
C: Homocysteine and hypersegmented neutrophils are shared by both.
D: Statements iii) and iv) occur in both deficiencies.
Takeaway: MMA plus homocysteine means B12. Homocysteine only means folate.

questions.p: Bruno, 58, has fatigue and an enlarged spleen. WBC is 180 with myelocytes, neutrophils, basophilia and eosinophilia, and only 1% blasts. FISH shows BCR-ABL. What is the main long-term treatment?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Basophilia, eosinophilia and a bimodal spread of myelocytes and neutrophils with BCR-ABL fit chronic phase CML. Chronic treatment is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as imatinib.
A: ATRA treats APL.
B: Lenalidomide is for MDS with del(5q) and myeloma.
C: Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells.
D: CML is treated, unlike low-risk CLL.
Takeaway: CML: Philadelphia chromosome, BCR-ABL, TKI.

questions.p: Mateo, 19, starts chemotherapy for a bulky lymphoma. Two days later he has palpitations and low urine output. Potassium, phosphate, urate and creatinine are high, and calcium is low. What is the best management?
o: A bisphosphonate infusion with IV hydration
questions.e:
Correct: D. High urate, potassium and phosphate with low calcium after chemotherapy is tumour lysis syndrome. Management is hydration, rasburicase or allopurinol, frequent labs and dialysis if needed.
A: Plasma exchange and steroids treat TTP.
B: Bisphosphonates treat hypercalcemia, and his calcium is low.
C: Leukapheresis treats leukostasis from a high blast count.
Takeaway: TLS: high K, PO4 and urate, low Ca.

questions.p: Victor, 55, has a lymphoma found only in his stomach. CT shows no enlarged lymph nodes and his marrow is clear. He has no fever, night sweats or weight loss. What is his Ann Arbor stage?
questions.e:
Correct: A. A single extralymphatic organ or site with no nodes is stage IE. No B symptoms gives the A suffix.
B: Stage II needs two or more node regions, or an extralymphatic site with nodes, on one side of the diaphragm.
C: B needs B symptoms.
D: Stage IV is diffuse extralymphatic involvement, such as marrow.
Takeaway: Stage I: one region or one extralymphatic site.

questions.p: Investigators compare a new oral drug with the standard IV drug. They expect it to work about as well, but it is easier to take and less toxic. Which trial design fits?
questions.e:
Correct: C. A non-inferiority trial shows that the new therapy is not clinically worse than the comparator. It suits a drug that may not work better but offers safety, tolerability or convenience.
A: A superiority trial expects the new drug to work better.
B: An equivalence trial shows the difference lies between a lower and an upper margin.
D: Phase 1 trials study safety and dose in 10 to 30 people.
Takeaway: The non-inferiority margin must be set in advance.

questions.p: Rosa, 31, has lupus. She is tired and jaundiced with an enlarged spleen. Hb is 86 g/L, reticulocytes are high and the film shows spherocytes and polychromasia. The direct antiglobulin test is positive for IgG. Which diagnosis fits best?
questions.e:
Correct: A. Spherocytes with a DAT positive for IgG point to warm AIHA. SLE is a listed cause, and warm antibodies bind at 37°C.
B: Hereditary spherocytosis also shows spherocytes, but its DAT is negative.
C: Cold AIHA has a DAT positive for C3 and shows agglutination.
D: G6PD deficiency shows bite cells and Heinz bodies with a negative DAT.
Takeaway: The DAT separates immune from non-immune hemolysis. IgG is warm, C3 is cold.

questions.p: Norma, 68, has an IgG kappa M protein, anemia and back pain. Which test is the standard of care to look for her bone disease?
questions.e:
Correct: B. Lytic lesions or fractures can show on XR, CT, PET-CT or MRI, and the skeletal survey is the standard of care.
A: Flow cytometry studies the marrow plasma cells.
C: The free light chain assay finds the M protein, not bone lesions.
D: A bone scan is listed for lymphoma bone involvement.
Takeaway: Myeloma bone disease: skeletal survey.

questions.p: Clifford, 72, has multiple myeloma with a creatinine of 210 µmol/L and a calcium of 2.9 mmol/L. What best explains his kidney injury?
o: Shiga toxin damages the glomerular endothelium
Antibodies form against heparin and platelet factor 4
Big sticky blasts block the small renal vessels
Abnormal protein and high calcium injure the kidney
questions.e:
Correct: D. In myeloma, abnormal protein and high calcium can damage the kidneys. Renal dysfunction is a medical emergency treated with anti-myeloma therapy and hemodialysis.
A: Shiga toxin causes HUS.
B: Anti-PF4 antibodies cause HIT.
C: Sticky blasts cause leukostasis in acute leukemia.
Takeaway: CRAB: calcium, renal, anemia, bone.

questions.p: Hector, 62, has a rapidly growing neck mass, night sweats and a high LDH. Biopsy shows diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and PET-CT shows stage IV disease. How should you counsel him?
o: Treated like Hodgkin, with ABVD then AVD
Incurable, so radiation alone is used for his symptoms
Aggressive but treatable, with 6 cycles of CHOP-R
Slow growing, so watch and wait until symptoms
questions.e:
Correct: C. DLBCL is aggressive and rapidly fatal untreated, but it responds well to treatment. Stage III to IV gets 6 cycles of CHOP-R. As in your Week 12 quiz, he is at risk of tumour lysis with chemotherapy.
A: ABVD and AVD are Hodgkin regimens.
B: DLBCL is treated with combination chemotherapy.
D: Watch and wait is for indolent follicular lymphoma.
Takeaway: DLBCL: aggressive, curable, CHOP-R.

questions.p: Ivan, 74, has new large bruises and no prior bleeding history. His aPTT is prolonged and his INR is normal. A 50:50 mix of his plasma with normal plasma does not correct the aPTT. What does this result suggest?
o: A platelet function disorder from aspirin
Multiple factor deficiencies from liver disease
An acquired inhibitor, such as anti-FVIII
A single factor deficiency, like hemophilia A
questions.e:
Correct: C. When the mix does not correct, an inhibitor is present. An acquired inhibitor against FVIII is a listed cause of an isolated high aPTT.
A: A platelet disorder leaves the INR and aPTT normal.
B: Multiple deficiencies give partial correction, and liver disease raises the INR as well.
D: A factor deficiency corrects with normal plasma.
Takeaway: Corrects: deficiency. Does not correct: inhibitor.

questions.p: Which statement about bone marrow sampling is correct?
o: Sternal aspirates are allowed, sternal cores are not
The tibia is an accepted aspirate site in adults
Core biopsies may be taken from the ribs
The PSIS is reserved for children and avoided in adults
questions.e:
Correct: A. The PSIS is the standard site. In extenuating circumstances the sternum can be used for an aspirate, but a core biopsy is never taken from the sternum because it is too close to the heart.
B: The tibia is used only in children.
C: Core biopsies are never taken from the ribs.
D: The PSIS is the standard site in adults and children, as in your Week 11 quiz.
Takeaway: Core biopsy: never sternum, tibia, skull or ribs.

questions.p: A 45-year-old has a smooth, fluid-filled mass in the middle mediastinum on CT. It looks like a simple bronchogenic cyst, and he has no symptoms. Which approach fits?
o: Scrotal ultrasound for a germ cell tumour
Surgical resection as for a thymoma
No biopsy for a simple cyst
questions.e:
Correct: D. Biopsy is skipped for a simple cyst, an aneurysm or a thymoma. A benign bronchogenic cyst is a middle compartment lesion.
A: Scrotal ultrasound looks for a germ cell tumour, an anterior mass.
B: Biopsy with flow cytometry is for suspected lymphoma or other malignancy.
C: Thymoma is an anterior mass that goes straight to resection.
Takeaway: No biopsy for a simple cyst, aneurysm or thymoma.

questions.p: Harold, 67, is on dialysis for chronic renal failure. Hb is 92 g/L with an MCV of 90 fL and a low reticulocyte count. Iron studies, B12 and folate are normal, and he is not bleeding. Which treatment best addresses his anemia?
questions.e:
Correct: B. A low reticulocyte count means a production problem. With normal iron and vitamins, chronic renal failure is the listed EPO indication, and EPO can raise Hb below 120 g/L.
A: Transfusion is for Hb below 70 g/L or symptomatic anemia.
C: His B12 is normal.
D: His iron studies are normal, so iron will not help.
Takeaway: EPO: renal failure, AIDS on antivirals, chemotherapy, pre-op care, MDS.

questions.p: Gerald, 56, does not drink alcohol. Hb is 118 g/L and MCV 106 fL. The film shows large round red cells, target cells and normal neutrophils. B12 and folate are normal. What is the most likely cause of his macrocytosis?
questions.e:
Correct: D. Large round red cells with normal neutrophils are non-megaloblastic. Target cells point to liver disease, and alcohol is only one of its causes.
A: Hypothyroidism is non-megaloblastic but is not a listed cause of target cells.
B: Folate deficiency is megaloblastic, and his folate is normal.
C: B12 deficiency gives oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils, and his B12 is normal.
Takeaway: Target cells: liver disease, hyposplenism, thalassemia.

questions.p: Raymond, 61, has a painful lesion in one rib. Biopsy shows a solid tumour of clonal plasma cells. His marrow, calcium, kidney function and Hb are normal, and imaging shows no other lesions. Which diagnosis and outlook fit?
o: Plasma cell leukemia, a medical emergency
questions.e:
Correct: C. A single solid myeloma tumour with no other disease is a solitary plasmacytoma, which has a good prognosis.
A: Multiple plasmacytomas mean end-stage disease, and he has one lesion.
B: Smoldering myeloma needs 10% or more marrow plasma cells, and his marrow is normal.
D: Plasma cell leukemia has plasma cells in the blood.
Takeaway: One plasmacytoma is good. Many is end stage.

questions.p: Marinette, 73, has months of painful, swollen joints that she has not had checked. Hb is 94 g/L, MCV 78 fL, ferritin 350 µg/L, transferrin saturation 13% and CRP 38 mg/L. She is not bleeding. Which plan best fits her anemia?
o: Transfuse red cells to an Hb above 120 g/L
Start oral iron to rebuild her iron stores
Arrange colonoscopy for occult GI blood loss
questions.e:
Correct: B. High ferritin with low transferrin saturation and a high CRP fits anemia of chronic inflammation, as in your Schulich review case. Therapy targets the underlying disease, and it seldom needs transfusion.
A: Anemia of chronic inflammation seldom requires a transfusion.
C: Her ferritin is high, so her stores are not depleted.
D: GI blood loss causes iron deficiency, which has a low ferritin.
Takeaway: Ferritin is high in chronic inflammation and low in iron deficiency.

questions.p: Leila, 38, has pancytopenia and bleeding gums. Her film shows immature cells with several Auer rods in the same cell. Which statement about her most likely diagnosis is correct?
o: Early deaths are usually from severe hemorrhage
Its blasts are HLA-DR positive on flow cytometry
It is confirmed by finding the t(9;22) translocation
First-line treatment is the TKI imatinib
questions.e:
Correct: A. Multiple Auer rods in one cell point to APL. APL has a high risk of early death, usually from severe hemorrhage, often in the brain.
B: APL blasts are HLA-DR negative.
C: APL is confirmed by t(15;17) or the PML/RARα fusion gene. t(9;22) is the Philadelphia chromosome of CML.
D: APL is treated with ATRA. Imatinib is for CML.
Takeaway: APL: Auer rods, DIC, start ATRA right away.

questions.p: Janice, 29, has been a strict vegan for 6 years. She has fatigue, poor concentration and tingling in her feet. Hb is 96 g/L, MCV 114 fL, WBC 3.5 and platelets 132. She takes an iron supplement. What is the best next step?
o: Refer urgently for a marrow biopsy for MDS
Type and screen for transfusion and admission
Start oral folate alone and recheck in a year
Start B12 replacement and repeat the CBC
questions.e:
Correct: D. A vegan diet is a listed cause of B12 deficiency, and stores last 3 to 4 years, so 6 years is enough to run out. Neuropathy with mild low counts fits B12 deficiency, which can cause neutropenia and thrombocytopenia.
A: MDS has a median age of 65 to 70, and her diet gives a clear cause first.
B: She is stable and well above the transfusion threshold of 70 g/L.
C: Folate does not replace B12, and her diet points to B12.
Takeaway: Vegan diet, neuropathy and macrocytosis: think B12.

questions.p: Kevin, 45, is 10 days out from chemotherapy. His temperature is 38.6°C, ANC is 0.2 and his central line site is red and tender. Blood cultures are drawn. Which antibiotic plan is best?
o: Oral antibiotics with outpatient review tomorrow
Hold antibiotics until cultures come back
questions.e:
Correct: C. A single temperature above 38.3°C with severe neutropenia is febrile neutropenia, an oncologic emergency. Start broad-spectrum antibiotics such as piperacillin-tazobactam, and add vancomycin for an IV catheter site infection.
A: Vancomycin must be added because of the catheter site infection.
B: Febrile neutropenia is an emergency treated with IV broad-spectrum antibiotics.
D: Antibiotics start empirically without waiting for cultures.
Takeaway: Febrile neutropenia is an oncologic emergency.

questions.p: Two women have a microcytic anemia. Woman A, 20, has Hb 112 g/L, MCV 58 fL and a uniform population of small red cells with target cells. Her ferritin is normal. Woman B, 35, has Hb 98 g/L, MCV 74 fL, a high RDW and a low ferritin. Which diagnosis fits each woman, in order?
questions.e:
Correct: B. Uniform microcytosis with target cells and a normal ferritin fits thalassemia, as in the Week 9 Jeopardy case. A high RDW with a low ferritin fits iron deficiency.
A: Woman A's ferritin is normal, which does not fit iron deficiency.
C: Anemia of chronic inflammation has a high ferritin, and Woman B's ferritin is low.
D: This reverses the two patterns. Iron deficiency is the one with a low ferritin.
Takeaway: Low ferritin and high RDW mean iron deficiency. Thalassemia is confirmed by hemoglobin electrophoresis.
